781.quote_or_event: “You took pity on me, and blessed me with Your Mercy, and I have met the True Guru, my Friend.”
781.explanation: Guru Arjan's closing salok calls the True Guru a friend (sajjan), and says such a friend is met only through God's mercy, not won by one's own merit.
781.tie_back: The Kural asks what is as hard to win as friendship; Guru Arjan says the truest friend is so hard to win that he comes only by grace.
781.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
781._accuracy_note: Captures the rarity of the true friend, but the friend is the Guru and the gift is spiritual; nothing here addresses friendship as a defence against enemies.

782.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool, and love with a pompous person, are like lines drawn in water, leaving no trace or mark.”
782.explanation: Guru Angad's saloks in Asa di Vaar warn that friendship with a fool never works out right and leaves nothing lasting behind.
782.tie_back: The Kural says friendship with fools wanes like the moon after the full; Guru Angad says it vanishes like a line drawn in water.
782.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
782._accuracy_note: A close match on the worthlessness of friendship with fools; it lacks the Kural's matching half on friendship with the wise growing like the crescent moon.

783.quote_or_event: “Kabir! The sandalwood tree is good, even though it is surrounded by weeds. Those who dwell near the sandalwood tree, become just like the sandalwood tree.”
783.explanation: Kabir uses the sandalwood tree to show how the company of the good gradually passes on its fragrance to those who keep near it.
783.tie_back: The Kural says the company of people of fine character gives more delight the longer one keeps it, like a great book; Kabir says those who stay close to the good slowly take on their fragrance.
783.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 11) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
783._accuracy_note: Shares the deepening benefit of good company, but Kabir's image is moral transformation, not the growing pleasure the Kural compares to rereading a book.

784.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak stayed at the inn of Sajjan at Tulamba, a man who posed as pious but robbed his guests. Instead of flattering his host, the Guru sang a hymn exposing hollow shininess (now in the Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729); Sajjan confessed, gave away his ill-gotten goods and turned his house into a dharamsala.
784.explanation: The story shows the Guru as a guest who took the initiative to confront a host's wrongdoing, and so saved him.
784.tie_back: The Kural says friendship exists so that we can step in first and rebuke a friend who goes too far; Guru Nanak's hymn to Sajjan was just such a timely rebuke that turned him back.
784.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Sajjan, Shaikh' and 'Tulamba' (paraphrase of the Janamsakhi tradition)
784._accuracy_note: A good example of corrective rebuke, but Janamsakhi stories are hagiography, the details vary between versions, and Sajjan was the Guru's host rather than an established friend.

785.quote_or_event: “Once united with Him, they will not be separated again, if they are truly united.”
785.explanation: Guru Nanak says that a union which is real does not come apart, because it rests on inner oneness rather than outward closeness.
785.tie_back: The Kural says friendship needs no constant meetings, only a shared understanding of heart; Guru Nanak likewise makes true union depend on inner oneness, which separation cannot undo.
785.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
785._accuracy_note: Only loosely parallel: the union meant is the soul's union with God, not like-mindedness between friends; no closer Sikh source was found.

786.quote_or_event: “They alone are true, whose love for God is deep and heart-felt. Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
786.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, sets heart-felt love against love that lives only on the lips.
786.tie_back: The Kural says friendship that only makes the face smile is not friendship, while friendship that makes the heart smile is; Farid likewise counts true only the love that is in the heart, not merely on the lips.
786.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
786._accuracy_note: A close match on inner versus outward love, though Farid speaks of love for God rather than between friends.

787.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
787.explanation: Guru Nanak's hymn (traditionally sung to Sajjan) defines true friends as those who stay with us right up to the moment of reckoning.
787.tie_back: The Kural says a friend shares our suffering when ruin comes; Guru Nanak's true friends still stand beside us when the account is called and judgement falls.
787.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
787._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the friend who stays through ruin, though the 'friends' are often read as one's good deeds and virtues before God, and the Kural's first two duties (turning a friend from ruin, guiding him) are not stated here.

788.quote_or_event: “Great is His greatness, as He gives without being asked.”
788.explanation: Guru Nanak praises God as the giver who meets our needs before we ask.
788.tie_back: The Kural's friendship, like a hand catching a slipping garment, removes a friend's distress at once, without being asked; Guru Nanak praises the same unasked help in God.
788.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
788._accuracy_note: Shares only the unasked help; it is about God's generosity, not a friend's instant reflex, so this is a next-best match.

789.quote_or_event: “My associates and companions have all deserted me; no one remains with me. Says Nanak, in this tragedy, the Lord alone is my Support.”
789.explanation: In this salok attributed to Guru Tegh Bahadur, human companions fall away in adversity, and only God stays as an unwavering support.
789.tie_back: The Kural places friendship's throne in steady, unwavering support; this salok shows by contrast how worldly companions waver, and finds that steady prop in God alone.
789.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 55), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
789._accuracy_note: A contrast more than a parallel: it shows the absence of the steady friend the Kural describes and finds that support only in God.

790.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! He alone is called a lover, who remains forever immersed in absorption. But one who feels good only when good is done for him, and feels bad when things go badly - do not call him a lover. He trades only for his own account.”
790.explanation: Guru Angad says that love which keeps track of what it receives is not love but trade.
790.tie_back: The Kural says friendship cheapens when friends measure and advertise what each is to the other; Guru Angad likewise calls love that keeps accounts mere trading.
790.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
790._accuracy_note: Strong on rejecting love that keeps accounts, matching Parimelazhagar's 'trader' reading, but it concerns love of God and does not address boasting about the friendship.
